newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mystery corpse may be key to Mexico murder scandal.
newsitem.headline: Mystery corpse may be key to Mexico murder scandal.

text.p: Mexican authorities claimed a breakthrough on Thursday in a murder investigation against the brother of former President Carlos Salinas after discovering a corpse on one of his ranches.
Salinas' defence lawyer dismissed the finding -- a body with its skull cut in two -- as a frame-up by prosecutors desperate to solve a scandal that has plagued Mexican politics for more than a year.

Attorney-General Antonio Lozano said the remains found on Wednesday could be those of Manuel Munoz Rocha, a key witness in the murder of a top ruling party politician in September 1994 who disappeared shortly afterward.

"If we prove the identity of these remains as those of Mr. Munoz Rocha and the cause of death (as murder) of course this will have a very important effect on the murder investigation," Lozano told Multivision Radio.
Lozano noted that Munoz Rocha was last seen alive by a witness who dropped him off in central Mexico City for a meeting with Raul Salinas.

In a move that shook Mexico, Raul Salinas was arrested in February 1995 and accused of masterminding the shooting of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, the number two in the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

Ruiz Massieu's assassination outside a Mexico City hotel was one of a chain of calamities that led to the December 1994 collapse of the Mexican peso, which plunged the country into its worst economic recession in 60 years.

The Excelsior newspaper on Thursday ran a front-page story saying a secret witness had told investigators that Raul himself smashed Munoz Rocha's skull with a baseball bat, then buried the body in the grounds of his ranch after having its fingers cut off and lower jaw removed to prevent identification.
The Attorney General's office had no comment on the report beyond saying that the skull found had suffered a heavy blow.

Raul has consistently maintained his innocence, saying he was jailed for political reasons. After more than a year of largely fruitless investigations, newspapers had speculated that he might be acquitted because detectives still lacked hard evidence to link him to the murder.

Raul's lawyer Eduardo Luengo followed that line again on Thursday, telling reporters the discovery of the body on the "El Encanto" (Charm) ranch on the edge of Mexico City was "another proof that the Attorney General's Office has been trying to build up a case about something for which they have no hard evidence."
Lozano, he added, "has launched a great crusade against the Salinas family and in particular against (Raul) Salinas."
The lawyer said the ranch had been taken over by prosecutors a year and a half ago and no one else had been allowed in.

Hair found with the body could have been planted by investigators who were given samples of Munoz Rocha's hair by his wife, Luengo added. He called for an independent examination of the remains to determine whose they were.

Mexican journalists, often suspicious of official investigations because of past experiences of manipulation, pointed to the fact that the skull was cut into two pieces and had a surgical incision around its circumference -- hardly what one would expect of a murder victim.

Questioned about the cut and the scepticism surrounding the find of the body, Lozano admitted that investigators were saddled with a poor reputation but insisted that he did have hard evidence against Raul.
The cut in the skull, he said, could have been part of a strategy to confuse police and make the remains harder to identify.
